PAPER: Journal of Productivity Analysis (2026) 65:5 https://doi.org/10.1007/s11123-025-00790-2 Flying high or falling short? markup and product differentiation in the U.S. airline industry (2002–2022) Emili Grifell-Tatjé1 · Charles Howell2 Received: 28 January 2025 / Accepted: 20 October 2025 © The Author(s) 2025 Abstract The U.S. airline industry experienced dramatic financial performance swings over the past two decades, moving from $31 billion in operating losses (2002–2009) to $163 billion in operating profits (2010–2019), followed by steep losses and a timid recovery during the pandemic (2020–2022). Building on the work of C.A.K. Lovell, this paper introduces a novel framework for decomposing annual markup changes over this period. A key contribution is the inclusion of product differentiation as an economic driver—an often-overlooked factor in traditional financial performance analyses. Using this methodology, we analyze profitability changes across 20 U.S. airlines from 2002 to 2022, offering new insights into the drivers of both industry-wide and firm-level performance dynamics. JSON: Name: markup_product_diff_airlines Title: Decomposing U.S. airline profitability dynamics (2002–2022) using DEA-estimated cost and non-standard revenue frontiers with output attributes Short Hypothesis: Accounting for measurable output attributes (first-class share, seating density, flight frequency) in joint DEA-based cost and non-standard revenue frontier decompositions significantly alters estimated contributions of cost, revenue, and productivity to airline profitability change between 2002 and 2022 compared to decompositions that omit attributes. Related Work: Existing approaches to firm-level profitability decomposition and productivity accounting use either parametric stochastic frontier methods or nonparametric DEA/Malmquist frameworks to estimate cost frontiers and total factor productivity changes. Prior work on revenue-side analysis introduced non-standard revenue functions that maximize prices given outputs, and Konüs-type index methods have been used to decompose price and cost changes. Limitations in the current literature include (a) omission of explicit, measurable output attributes from cost and revenue frontiers, (b) reliance on CRS/VRS assumptions that do not capture heterogeneous scale regimes, (c) limited integration of revenue-frontier results with cost-frontier decompositions to produce a monetary profitability decomposition, and (d) sensitivity of frontier estimates to endogeneity and extreme shocks. Empirical airline studies have documented industry-level swings but have not systematically quantified the joint impact of product differentiation on cost, revenue, and profitability decomposition. Abstract: This project develops and empirically implements a joint decomposition of profitability change that integrates output-attribute-aware cost frontiers with non-standard revenue frontiers to quantify the role of product differentiation in the U.S. airline industry (2002–2022). Methodologically, we estimate sequential, generalized-returns-to-scale (GRS) DEA input-minimizing cost frontiers that include observable output attributes (first-class share, seating density, flight frequency) and DEA-based non-standard revenue frontiers that maximize achievable prices conditional on outputs, input prices and attributes. We then produce a multiplicative decomposition of changes in the revenue-to-cost (markup) ratio into attribute, efficiency, technical (frontier), activity, and input-price components. The primary contribution is a replicable, monetary-level decomposition showing how measurable product differentiation affects both sides of the firm ledger and alters inferred productivity and markup drivers. We expect the approach to reveal nontrivial attribute contributions to profitability swings and to improve attribution accuracy relative to models that omit attributes. Experiments: Datasets: DOT Form 41 annualized operating and financial data (1998–2022 full panel; analysis 2002–2022), DB1B ticket-sample variables for first/business class share, OAG or DOT schedules for route-level departures to compute average frequency, aircraft/seat inventories for seating density, fuel price series (US Gulf Coast jet kerosene). Sample: all U.S. carriers with consistent Form 41 reporting across 2002–2022 (target N ≈ 20 carriers, balanced panel). Preprocessing: deflate nominal values by CPI; compute quantities and unit prices for inputs (capital, labor, fuel, other) and outputs (revenue-passenger-miles, freight ton-miles); construct attribute vectors q = {first_class_share, seat_density^{-1}, avg_daily_departures}. Baselines: (B1) DEA cost and NSRF revenue without attributes (standard sequential CRS and VRS); (B2) Parametric SFA cost + OLS/GLS revenue specification with attributes; (B3) DEA cost with attributes but using CRS/VRS instead of GRS. Primary method: sequential GRS DEA (input-orientation) to estimate c(w,y,q) and DEA NSRF to estimate r(w,y,q); implement multiplicative decomposition of Π_{t+1}/Π_t into QPI (attribute profit index), efficiency and technical (cost & revenue), activity and input-price factors as specified in expression (11). Parameters: GRS intensity bounds set to L=0.5, U=2.0; sequential technology pool starts 1998; DEA solved annually for each firm-year. Evaluation metrics: (1) percentage contribution of each decomposition component to aggregate profitability change; (2) paired statistical comparison (paired t-test and Wilcoxon signed-rank) of component magnitudes between primary method and each baseline; (3) frontier fit diagnostics: mean DEA slacks, root-mean-square of input slacks, and outlier influence measures; (4) bootstrap (n=1000) confidence intervals for decomposition components; (5) variance decomposition: fraction of cross-sectional variance in profitability change explained by attribute vs non-attribute components. Ablations and robustness: (A1) drop each attribute individually to obtain marginal contribution; (A2) repeat with CRS and VRS to quantify sensitivity to return-to-scale assumption; (A3) restrict sample by period (2002–2009, 2010–2019, 2020–2022) to compare pre/post effects and pandemic sensitivity; (A4) test for endogeneity by correlating DEA efficiency scores with attributes and by estimating 2SLS regressions where feasible. Implementation: linear programming solvers for DEA (e.g., cplex/gurobi or high-performance open-source LP) with scripts in R/Python; report p-values, bootstrap CIs, and effect sizes for all comparisons. Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Measurement error and sampling bias: DB1B ticket-sample and schedule aggregation can mis-measure first-class share, frequency and density, biasing attribute effects. 2) Endogeneity: attributes may be jointly determined with prices and unobserved demand shocks, producing biased DEA/NSRF efficiency and frontier estimates. 3) DEA sensitivity: frontier estimates are sensitive to outliers, small-sample firms, and the choice of GRS bounds (L,U); results may be unstable for carriers with few observations. 4) Sequential-technology assumption: sequential pooling assumes no technical regress and that historical observations are comparable; violations (structural breaks, discontinuous regime shifts) can invalidate inferences. 5) Pandemic and extreme shocks: 2020–2022 observations are outliers that can dominate decomposition unless separately analyzed, reducing generalizability. 6) Computational cost: bootstrap for DEA/NSRF with large LPs and 1000 replications may require high compute resources. 7) External validity: results from the U.S. market and selected attributes may not generalize to other countries, international routes, or other attribute specifications. 8) Collinearity: attributes may be correlated with each other and with outputs, complicating marginal attribution and interpretation.
